This research aims to delve deeper into the paradox by examining the level or extent of young people’s reliance on such AI chatbots for emotional assistance and social interaction and how this dependence may unintentionally contribute to attachments with AI chatbots

item.title: The Psychology of Generative AI Dependence: Reward, PsychologicalNeeds, and the Emerging Architecture of Problematic Human–AIEngagement
item.description:
Journal of Psychiatry Research Reviews & Reports
The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the relationship between humans and digital technology. Unlike digital systems that primarily delivered information, mediated interpersonal communication, or provided entertainment, generative AI can respond conversationally, personalise interactions, produce immediate solutions, simulate empathy, reduce cognitive effort, and remain continuously available. These characteristics raise an emerging question: can repeated engagement with generative AI develop into psychologically dependent or addiction-like patterns, and, if so, through what mechanisms? This paper employs an integrative critical literature review and conceptual synthesis to examine problematic generative-AI use through the combined perspectives of behavioural addiction theory, reward and reinforcement processes, the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model, self-determination theory, compensatory technology use, social anxiety, loneliness, anthropomorphism, cognitive offloading, and human psychological needs. The current study identifies a major gap in the current literature: emerging research frequently examines AI dependence as either a behavioural outcome, an educational problem, or a form of social attachment, but insufficiently integrates the neuropsychological processes of reinforcement with the psychological needs that make generative AI personally rewarding. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Need–Reward–Dependence (NRD) Framework, according to which problematic GenAI engagement develops through the interaction of three processes: unmet or salient psychological needs, rapid need-contingent reinforcement delivered by AI, and repeated cognitive or emotional outsourcing that strengthens habitual reliance. The framework proposes that competence, relatedness, autonomy, reassurance, emotional regulation, cognitive ease, social safety, and control can act as psychologically rewarding affordances of generative AI. Repeated reinforcement may increase cue-reactivity, habitual checking, perceived indispensability, cognitive delegation, emotional attachment, and impaired self-regulation in susceptible users. Importantly, this paper does not claim that generative-AI addiction is currently established as a distinct psychiatric disorder. Rather, it argues that a theoretically coherent and increasingly empirically observable continuum exists from adaptive use through reliance and dependence to potentially compulsive engagement associated with functional impairment. The paper concludes that future research should distinguish productive high-frequency use from clinically meaningful problematic use and should examine the interaction between users’ psychological vulnerabilities and the reward architecture of generative-AI systems

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Analytics: An Integrative Review of Financial Modeling, Forecasting, and Financial Controls
item.description:
Journal of Applied Finance and Banking
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied across finance, including fraud detection, risk assessment, and forecasting, yet forecasting and internal controls are often governed in separate initiatives. This paper examines two pillars of AI use in finance: AI-driven financial modeling and forecasting, and AI-driven reconciliation within internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The paper is based on a literature review of 23 academic, regulatory, and standards sources, including materials from the SEC, PCAOB, and COSO. The review indicates that the two pillars are interdependent: reconciled, well-governed data underpins reliable forecasting, and continuous reconciliation combined with predictive modeling can support pre-filing risk detection in SEC reporting. Model risk management, explainability, and human sign-off emerge as governance requirements common to both pillars. Building on these insights, the paper proposes a five-stage maturity framework that sequences AI-driven reconciliation ahead of predictive forecasting, together with shared governance practices. The findings suggest that managing forecasting and controls under a unified governance approach offers a coherent pathway for AI adoption in finance. JEL classification numbers: C53, G17, G32, M41, M42. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Finance, Financial Analytics, Automated Reconciliation, Internal Controls, AI-Driven Finance.

item.title: Thayer-inspired teaching routines as active learning in higher business education
item.description:
[预印本] Instituto Politécnico do Porto
This paper reports an embedded case study of a Thayer-inspired teaching routine (M1–M2–M3) implemented across four business curricular units (covering global competitiveness, strategic marketing, international marketing, and B2B marketing) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The routine operationalises (M1) a 10–20 minutes conceptual framing with explicit learning outcomes; (M2) small-group (≤3 students) applied problem work using permitted digital tools (including AI under disclosure and verification rules); and (M3) an unsupported oral defence (no slides, notes, or devices), with mandatory individual contribution and structured questioning. Drawing on evidence on active learning effectiveness and constructive alignment, the M1–M2–M3 routine is conceptualised as integrity-by-design: students may use tools to learn and build artefacts (M2), while their individual understanding and reasoning are authenticated through a technology-free defence (M3). Across the four embedded units of analysis, findings report a trajectory from initial student discomfort and insufficient preparation to progressively stronger conceptual accuracy and argumentation. The paper documents the positive learning outcomes achieved and the structural challenges encountered (including anxiety, overload, and unequal academic capital) and discusses their implications for assessment design in AI-normalised environments

item.title: How AI-Enabled Service Encounters Shape Tourist Trust: The Role of Perceived Personalization and Interactional Justice
item.description:
Journal of theoretical and applied electronic commerce research
As Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies increasingly mediate service encounters in tourism, understanding how AI-enabled interactions shape tourist trust has become a pressing issue. Drawing on social exchange theory and justice theory, this study investigates the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI service quality influences tourist trust. Using the AI digital human Wang Bo at the Tengwang Pavilion scenic area as an empirical case, the research develops and tests a model in which perceived personalization and interactional justice act as parallel mediators, while privacy sensitivity and brand reputation serve as moderators. Results from structural equation modeling show that AI service quality significantly enhances both perceived personalization and interactional justice, which in turn foster tourist trust. Perceived personalization and interactional justice each play significant mediating roles, indicating that tourists’ trust in AI arises not merely from technical performance but from perceptions of individualized care and fair treatment. Among the moderating effects, privacy sensitivity attenuates the relationship between AI service quality and interactional justice but does not affect the link between AI service quality and perceived personalization. Brand reputation strengthens the impact of perceived personalization on trust but does not significantly moderate the relationship between interactional justice and trust. Overall, the findings reveal dual pathways—personalization-based and fairness-based—through which AI service quality builds trust, highlighting the interplay between technological excellence, human-like social attributes, and contextual factors in shaping tourists’ trust toward AI-enabled services. This study advances theoretical understanding of AI-mediated service relationships and offers practical insights for designing trustworthy AI experiences in tourism contexts.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Firm Value: The Moderating Role of Board Independence: Evidence from Saudi Listed Firms
item.description:
Journal of risk and financial management
This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) disclosure and firm value and investigates the moderating role of board independence among Saudi listed non-financial firms over 2019–2025. A multidimensional Artificial Intelligence Disclosure Intensity Index (AIDI) is developed to capture the breadth and substantive depth of AI-related corporate reporting across five dimensions. Using an unbalanced panel of 145 firms and 930 firm-year observations (785 in the estimation sample), the study employs panel regression and dynamic System GMM, with Tobin’s Q as the primary measure of firm value. The findings show a positive association between AI disclosure intensity and firm value, conditional on the included controls. We also find positive associations using alternative disclosure measures, accounting-based performance outcomes, firm fixed effects, and System GMM; however, the one-year lagged AIDI coefficient is statistically insignificant. The study finds no statistically significant evidence of moderation by board independence. The study contributes to the emerging AI disclosure literature by providing a multidimensional disclosure measure and new evidence from the Saudi capital market. The results provide evidence of an association between reported AI disclosure and firm valuation, without establishing causality or investors’ responses to report publication.

item.title: From Social Interaction to Occupational Engagement: Evaluating the Role of Social Robots in Meaningful Activities for Older Adults
item.description:
Applied Sciences
(1) Background: Population ageing highlights the need for interventions promoting meaningful participation and occupational engagement. Social robots may support engagement in meaningful activities, but evidence addressing occupational engagement remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the role of an animal-like social robot in facilitating occupational engagement among older adults. (2) Methods: A longitudinal single-group pre–post study was conducted with 60 cognitively intact older adults attending day centres. Participants engaged in meaningful social, leisure, cognitive, creative, and activity-based experiences incorporating the MetaCat Smart Robot Cat twice weekly for three months, with 30–40 min sessions. Occupational engagement was assessed using the Engagement in Meaningful Activities Survey, while occupational performance and satisfaction were evaluated using the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure. Human–robot interaction was also monitored. (3) Results: EDIAS scores increased significantly after the intervention (mean change: 4.4 points; 95% CI: 3.4–5.4; p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 0.82), alongside improvements in occupational performance and satisfaction. Spontaneous interaction initiation and persistence increased over time and were positively associated with occupational engagement. (4) Conclusions: Animal-like social robots may facilitate occupational engagement when embedded in meaningful activities. Controlled studies are needed to establish causal effects.

item.title: Interpretable driver behavioral state monitoring using facial landmarks for human-autonomous vehicle interaction
item.description:
Frontiers in Robotics and AI
Introduction Behavior-aware robotic systems require both accurate human state recognition and transparent machine intent to support trust and safe collaboration. This study presents an integrated framework for autonomous vehicles combining a real-time vehicle state visualization interface with a calibration-driven facial-based behavioral state recognition module. Methods A Polaris GEM e6 autonomous vehicle equipped with drive-by-wire control and LiDAR served as the testbed. A real-time Human-Machine Interface (HMI) built with ROS and Foxglove Studio visualized localization, object detection, and driving states. Concurrently, a vision-based behavioral monitoring system used an Intel RealSense L515 camera, MediaPipe, and OpenCV to extract facial landmarks. Individual calibration established neutral baselines for eye aspect ratio, mouth aspect ration, and head rotation angles. A real-time threshold-based finite-state model facilitated data collection across five behavioral states: neutral, closed eyes, out-of-safe-zone, yawning, and fast blinking. Classical classifiers (Support Vector Machine [SVM], Random Forest [RF]), and deep learning architectures (Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks) were trained on a controlled indoor dataset using stratified k-fold cross-validation (k = 10), and evaluated on a hold-out outdoor dataset. Results The HMI provided stable, real-time visualization of vehicle state and perception, while the facial monitoring system achieved a ∼ 98.5% face detection success rate. The online heuristic model identified behavioral states and enabled high-quality data collection, capturing features with strong Kruskal-Wallis significance from the neutral state for closed eyes (EAR, p < 0.001 ), yawning (MAR, p < 0.001 ), fast blinking (blink rate, p < 0.01 ), though out-of-safe-zone was non-significant (head rotation, p > 0.05 ). Stratified cross-validation accuracy and F1-scores reached ∼ 91% for SVM and RF. On the outdoor test data, SVM maintained its performance, whereas RF dropped to a ∼ 70% F1-score due to inter-session variability and feature ambiguity. Deep learning architectures achieved test F1-scores ( ∼ 80%), comparable to the heuristic baseline model ( ∼ 81%). SVM was the most stable and best performing classifier, isolating its confusion to the out-of-safe-zone and neutral states. Conclusion Combining transparent interface design with personalized calibration supports human-aware autonomy. The machine learning framework provided interpretable monitoring, while real-time visualization enhanced situational awareness, together contributing to behaviorally responsive and transparent human-robot interaction platforms.

item.title: When support becomes dependence: conversational continuity and relational safety in human-AI interaction
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychiatry
Background Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support, reflection, and consequential decision-making. Although conversational continuity may improve responsiveness, sustained interaction also exposes AI systems to their own prior relational language, potentially shaping how they respond when users become increasingly dependent or surrender personal agency. We examined whether model-generated conversational history alters relational-safety behavior as human–AI interactions escalate from ordinary support-seeking toward emotional dependence, social displacement, and decision delegation. Methods We conducted a standardized multi-turn benchmarking study of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twelve four-turn trajectories represented two agency-related domains: emotional dependency and displacement of human support, and decision delegation and surrender of personal agency. Each trajectory was evaluated under two matched context architectures: reconstructed cumulative user-only context, which retained all prior user disclosures but excluded previous AI responses, and native continuous conversation, which retained the complete interaction history. Across 72 model-condition-trajectory sequences comprising 288 turn-level responses, relational safety was independently evaluated for dependency reinforcement, agency preservation, and human-support preservation using predefined ordinal criteria. Context effects and their interaction with escalating relational risk were examined using cumulative-link mixed-effects models. Results Relational-safety differences between context architectures increased across successive turns of the standardized trajectories. Overall, explicit dependency reinforcement increased from 9.7% in cumulative user-only contexts to 18.1% in continuous conversations, while strong agency preservation declined from 75.7% to 65.3% and strong human-support preservation from 73.6% to 63.2%. Outcome-specific analyses showed condition-by-turn interactions for dependency reinforcement (cumulative odds ratio [cOR], 1.26; 95% CI, 1.03–1.55; unadjusted P = .026), agency preservation (cOR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69–0.98; unadjusted P = .031), and human-support preservation (cOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65–0.94; unadjusted P = .009), indicating progressively greater divergence between context conditions across successive turns. After Holm adjustment across the three interaction tests, only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold (adjusted P = .027).The overall pattern was observed across systems and was directionally consistent in predefined binary sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Across this benchmark, between-condition differences generally widened across successive turns, although the present design cannot determine whether this pattern reflects increasing relational-risk intensity, increasing accumulated model-generated history, or their combination. Only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold after Holm adjustment, whereas the dependency-reinforcement and agency-preservation interactions were directionally similar but less robust after multiplicity adjustment. The observed pattern is compatible with a post-hoc interpretive framework of relational inertia but does not establish this process as a causal mechanism or demonstrate downstream psychological effects in human users.

item.title: If it doesn’t have a soul, it doesn’t hurt? The effect of bullying and social anxiety on the use of conversational AI
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) increasingly functions as a social interaction partner, raising questions about how established interpersonal behaviors transfer to human-AI interaction. The present study examined whether bullying-like behavior directed toward CAI reflects the extension of real world social strategies, and how social anxiety, prior bullying experiences, and AI self-competency contribute to such behavior. Methods Participants ( N = 289) completed measures of social anxiety, prior bullying perpetration and victimization, AI self-competency, and bullying-like behavior directed toward conversational AI. Results Through several analyses, bully-victims exhibited the highest levels of AI-directed bullying-like behavior. The interaction between bullying perpetration and victimization emerged as the strongest predictor in our regression analysis, while prior bullying perpetration alone was not sufficient to explain AI-directed aggression, and prior victimization alone was negatively associated with AI-directed bullying-like behavior. Social anxiety did not directly predict bullying-like behavior toward AI; however, mediation analyses showed that prior victimization fully mediated the relationship between social anxiety and bullying-like behavior towards CAI. Individuals with higher social anxiety were more likely to report victimization, which in turn was associated with increased bullying-like behavior toward AI. AI self-competency did not emerge as an independent predictor. Discussion These findings suggest that AI-directed bullying-like behavior is best understood as a context-dependent behavior arising from the co-occurrence of aggression and vulnerability, rather than a direct extension of general aggressive tendencies. Conversational AI constitutes a distinct relational context that can both reflect and reinforce existing behavioral patterns. This has important implications for understanding how human-AI interactions may shape social behavior and psychological functioning over time.

item.title: The Dual Nature of AI-Supported Medical Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework of Efficiency, Responsibility, and Human–AI Collaboration
item.description:
Journal of Management Policy and Practice
In the medical field, while AI-driven systems promise enhanced efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and operational effectiveness, they also raise critical concerns about responsibility, accountability, and ethical judgment. Despite the growing body of empirical research on medical AI, limited attention has been given to the theoretical implications of AI integration from a management and organizational perspective. Our study develops a conceptual framework to explain the dual nature of AI-supported medical decision-making by integrating insights from decision-making theory, algorithmic management, and healthcare management literature. We propose that AI simultaneously enhances decision efficiency while creating new forms of responsibility ambiguity and ethical tension. The framework conceptualizes how AI capability, human–AI interaction, and organizational governance jointly shape decision outcomes, professional accountability, and organizational trust. By offering a theoretically grounded model, this study contributes to literature in three ways. First, it extends traditional decision-making theory to AI-augmented healthcare contexts. Second, it introduces responsibility as a central construct in human–AI collaboration. Third, it provides a foundation for future empirical research and managerial practice in healthcare organizations navigating AI adoption.

item.title: Toward Evidence-Based Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Cross-Domain Systematic Review
item.description:

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

item.title: Generative artificial intelligence in the preparation of scientific medical articles on surgery: principles of responsible use and current requirements of editorial organisations
item.description:
The Ukrainian Journal of Clinical Surgery
Background. The rapid adoption of large language models between 2022 and 2026 has transformed the routine preparation of scientific manuscripts. In surgery, where the author is simultaneously a practising clinician with limited time for analytical work and is often compelled to publish results in English, the temptation to delegate text preparation to generative tools is particularly high. At the same time, leading editorial organisations have restricted the permissible scenarios for the use of artificial intelligence and tightened the requirements for disclosing such use.Objective. To systematise the current positions of editorial organisations regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence in scientific manuscripts, to outline the functional classes of tools relevant to surgical writing, and to formulate a practical framework for the responsible use of artificial intelligence, suitable for implementation in a surgeon’s daily scientific work.Materials and methods. A narrative literature review involving a targeted search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar databases for the period from January 2022 to July 2026, with restrictions on language (English, Ukrainian) and source type (peer-reviewed articles, official position papers from editorial organisations, and guidance documents on disclosure). The formal PRISMA–ScR protocol was not applied.Results. The ICMJE, COPE and WAME have agreed on three key positions regarding artificial intelligence: artificial intelligence cannot be an author; human authors bear full responsibility for the accuracy, integrity and originality of scientific manuscripts; and the use of artificial intelligence must be disclosed. The main clinically significant risks are the fabrication of references, factual inaccuracies in a medical context, bias, model drift, lack of reproducibility and breaches of patient data confidentiality. Automated detectors and expert assessment of content generated using artificial intelligence have limited reliability, which highlights the importance of voluntary disclosure of the use of artificial intelligence.Conclusions. Generative artificial intelligence should be regarded as an editorial and structural tool rather than a source of evidence. Responsible use of artificial intelligence requires mandatory verification of every statement and reference, de-identification of data, compliance with applicable guidelines on reporting, and transparent disclosure in the ‘Methods’ and ‘Acknowledgements’ sections.
